title: Argument Is War
why: English talks about disagreement as if it were combat. Noticing this helps you follow meetings, debates and the news, and lets you choose a calmer framing when you want one.
know: the conceptual metaphor ARGUMENT IS WAR and where the idea comes from
eight high-frequency idioms of attack, defence and peace-making
understand: why words like attack, defend and win feel completely normal in a debate
which of these idioms are casual, neutral or slightly critical
able: use the idioms accurately and in the right register
vary the expressions the way native speakers do without breaking them
notice when military language makes a discussion more hostile than it needs to be
mistakes: We need to bite the bullet of the price increase.
We need to bite the bullet and accept the price increase. Bite the bullet takes no object.
She stuck to her weapons in the meeting.
She stuck to her guns. The noun is fixed: always guns.
Let's bury the axe and move on.
Let's bury the hatchet. Don't swap in a synonym.
We'll fight fire with fire. The point is using your opponent's own method.
The minister bit the bullet, stuck to her guns and shot down the critics' fort.
The minister stuck to her guns. Stacking war idioms sounds like a parody; one is enough.
bigidea: In Metaphors We Live By (1980), linguist George Lakoff and philosopher Mark Johnson used ARGUMENT IS WAR as their first example of a conceptual metaphor: a whole way of thinking that shows up in ordinary words, not just in poetry.
We say a claim is indefensible, a critic attacked a weak point, and someone won the argument. Nobody hears these as figurative; they are simply how English describes disagreement.

The frame has consequences. If debate is war, the other person is an enemy and changing your mind is defeat. Lakoff and Johnson asked readers to imagine a culture where argument is a dance. Skilled speakers can switch frames: explore an idea, build on a point, meet halfway.
hidden: The professor demolished my argument in about two minutes.
You can never win an argument with my brother.
The lawyer found a weak point in the testimony and targeted it.
The senator defended her position for over an hour.
He retreated from his earlier claim when the data came out.

expressions.meaning: refuse to change your opinion or plan despite pressure
expressions.example: Everyone said the café would fail, but she stuck to her guns and it's thriving.
expressions.bend: Change the tense and possessive: he stuck to his guns, we're sticking to our guns. Keep guns plural.
expressions.note: Usually approving. Compare dig your heels in, which suggests stubbornness rather than conviction.

expressions.meaning: force yourself to do something unpleasant that can't be avoided
expressions.example: We finally bit the bullet and replaced the furnace before winter.
expressions.bend: Often followed by and + verb: bite the bullet and call him. Tense changes freely; no object after bullet.
expressions.note: Don't confuse it with dodge a bullet (escape harm). Learners mix them up because both contain bullet.

expressions.example: The firm I almost joined went bankrupt in March. I really dodged a bullet.
expressions.bend: We dodged a bullet, that was a bullet dodged, dodged a big bullet. Usually past tense, looking back.
expressions.note: Often said with relief about a lucky escape, even a relationship: you dodged a bullet with him. British speakers also say a narrow escape.

expressions.meaning: (of a group) unite to protect one another from criticism
expressions.example: When the scandal broke, the board closed ranks around the CEO.
expressions.bend: Close ranks around or behind someone; any tense. Keep ranks plural and with no article.
expressions.note: In news writing it is often mildly critical: insiders protecting one of their own instead of being open.

expressions.meaning: something that has both a clear benefit and a related drawback
expressions.example: Working from home is a double-edged sword: no commute, but no clear end to the day.
expressions.bend: A fixed noun phrase. Natural frames: something of a double-edged sword, proved a double-edged sword.
expressions.note: Best when the advantage itself causes the harm. If the pros and cons are unrelated, just say it has pros and cons.

expressions.meaning: reject an idea or proposal firmly and quickly
expressions.example: I suggested a four-day week, but my manager shot it down in seconds.
expressions.bend: Separable: shoot down the idea or shoot it down. The passive is very common: my plan got shot down.
expressions.note: A little blunt. In formal writing prefer reject or dismiss. Related: shoot holes in an argument.

expressions.meaning: end a quarrel and become friendly again
expressions.example: After years of silence, the two brothers buried the hatchet at their mother's birthday.
expressions.bend: Any tense or subject: it's time to bury the hatchet. Keep hatchet; never axe.
expressions.note: Usually linked to peace customs of Indigenous nations in northeastern North America, where weapons were buried to mark the end of hostilities.

expressions.meaning: respond to an attack by using the same methods as the attacker
expressions.example: When the rival campaign ran attack ads, ours decided to fight fire with fire.
expressions.bend: Usually in the base form after decide to, have to, you can't. The wording is fixed.
expressions.note: Can sound like a justification for bad behaviour. The opposite choice is to take the high road.

culture.how: Shakespeare gave English hoist with his own petard. Hamlet arranges for the men sent to betray him to be destroyed by their own plot. A petard was a small bomb for blasting open gates, so the image is an engineer blown up by his own device: caught in your own trap.
culture.ask: Can you think of a politician, company or celebrity who was hoist with their own petard?
culture.find: hoist with his own petard Hamlet meaning

culture.how: After Caesar's murder, Mark Antony imagines war being released like hunting dogs straining at the leash. The phrase let slip the dogs of war comes from this speech, and journalists still use it for the start of a conflict, military or political.
culture.ask: Why is an image of hunting dogs so effective for the moment a war begins?
culture.find: let slip the dogs of war Julius Caesar Mark Antony

culture.how: The title carries the war frame from debate into romance: a relationship becomes a place of combat, with power struggles, wounds and survival. It shows how easily one conceptual metaphor spreads into new areas of life.
culture.ask: Do people in your first language talk about love as a kind of war? What other metaphors do they use for it?
culture.find: Pat Benatar Love Is a Battlefield

culture.how: The title uses the language of holding a position under fire. The song is about refusing to give in to pressure, the same idea as stick to your guns or hold the fort, which is why it has been popular at rallies and sports events.
culture.ask: When is refusing to back down admirable, and when is it just stubbornness?
culture.find: Tom Petty I Won't Back Down

culture.how: Owen, a British officer killed a week before the 1918 Armistice, describes a gas attack in the First World War. The poem rejects the old idea that dying for your country is sweet and glorious. It is a sober reminder of the real suffering behind our casual war idioms.
culture.ask: Does the reality of war change how you feel about phrases like win an argument or shoot down an idea?
culture.find: Wilfred Owen Dulce et Decorum Est

match.why: Like soldiers who stay at their guns instead of retreating.
You accept the pain because there is no way around it.
The bullet missed you. Usually said looking back with relief.
Soldiers move closer together so there are no gaps to attack.

match.r: a benefit with a built-in drawback
match.why: A blade sharp on both sides can cut the person holding it.
The idea is like an aircraft brought down before it can fly.
Burying a weapon means you no longer intend to fight.
You answer aggression with the same kind of aggression.

sort.h: Put each expression in the right group: does it describe holding your position, attacking, or escaping or ending the fight?

items.why: You stay where you are and refuse to retreat.
You keep things going and protect your position while others are away.
The group pulls together to defend itself.
You refuse to move or change your mind.
You actively destroy someone else's proposal.
You hit back using the same aggressive methods.
You stop defending and start attacking.
You choose a target to criticise.
Both sides agree to stop fighting.

You escape harm without fighting at all.
You surrender and end the fight by giving up.

pick.why: Bite the bullet = make yourself do something unpleasant. Dodging a bullet would mean escaping it.

pick.why: You escaped a loss by luck and timing: dodge a bullet.

pick.q: When reporters asked about the missing funds, the other officers ___ and refused to comment.
pick.why: The group united to protect a colleague: close ranks.

pick.q: Social media is ___ for small businesses: free advertising, but one bad review can go viral.
pick.why: The same tool helps and hurts, so it is a double-edged sword.

pick.q: The committee seemed interested in my proposal, but the finance director ___ within five minutes.
pick.why: She quickly rejected the idea: shot it down.

pick.q: The neighbours had argued about the fence for years, but they finally ___ over a barbecue.
pick.why: They ended the quarrel and became friendly: buried the hatchet.

pick.q: Critics demanded she cancel the exhibition, but the curator ___ and it opened on schedule.
pick.why: She refused to change her plan under pressure: stuck to her guns.

pick.q: If the other team is going to play dirty, we'll have to ___.
pick.why: Answering their tactics with the same tactics is fighting fire with fire.

spot.q: After the election the party leaders agreed to bury the axe and work together.
spot.why: The idiom is fixed: bury the hatchet. Swapping in a synonym breaks it.

spot.q: My boss shot up my idea before I could even finish explaining it.
spot.why: To reject an idea is to shoot it down. Shoot up means rise fast.

spot.q: We kept postponing the renovation, but last spring we bit the bomb and started.
spot.why: Bite the bullet = do the unpleasant thing. Bite the dust means fail or die.

spot.q: For young families, cheap credit is a two-edged knife.
spot.why: The set phrase is a double-edged sword. A two-way street means something mutual.

spot.q: Despite the angry emails, the principal stuck to her weapons and kept the new timetable.
spot.why: Always guns: stick to your guns. Stick your neck out means take a risk.

type.q: The minister had to bite the ___ and admit the figures were wrong.
type.why: Bite the bullet: accept something painful you can't avoid.

type.q: For young athletes, sudden fame can be a double-edged ___.
type.why: A double-edged sword: the benefit carries its own risk.

type.q: When one nurse was blamed, the whole ward closed ___ to protect her.
type.why: Close ranks: unite in defence. Plural, no article.

type.q: I nearly bought that house by the river before the flood. I dodged a ___.
type.why: Dodge a bullet: a narrow escape, said with relief.

type.q: It's been twenty years. Isn't it time you two buried the ___?
type.why: Bury the hatchet: make peace after a long quarrel.

type.q: The coach told us to fight fire with ___ and match their aggression.
type.why: Fight fire with fire: respond with the same methods.

bend.q: Which version sounds natural for a past event? ___
opts: Our proposal got shot over by the board.
Our proposal got shot down by the board.
Our proposal got shooting down by the board.
bend.why: Passive with get is very common: got shot down. The particle down can't change.

bend.q: Which version sounds natural about a whole group? ___
opts: The players are all sticking to their guns.
The players are all sticking to their gun.
The players are all sticking at their guns.
bend.why: Change the possessive and tense freely, but keep to and plural guns.

bend.q: Which version is a natural variation of the idiom? ___
opts: Fame turned out to be a sword with double edges.
Fame turned out to be a double-edged swords.
Fame turned out to be something of a double-edged sword.
bend.why: Something of softens the phrase naturally. Reordering the words or adding s breaks it.

bend.q: Which version sounds natural after a long argument? ___
opts: Let's bury a hatchet and move on.
Let's hide the hatchet and move on.
Let's bury the hatchet and move on.
bend.why: Bury and the are fixed. Only the tense and subject change.

What in modern life is a double-edged sword? Give two examples and explain both edges.
